claims.source: In cases in which BLA→GCx impacted >1 taste response (63 out of 78 neurons; the solid portion of Figure 3D), the perturbation either consistently suppressed (57.1%: 36 out of 63) or consistently enhanced (42.9%: 27 out of 63) response magnitudes for all affected taste responses (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: If a given neuron's activity was significantly altered by BLA→GCx, the direction of impact (suppression/enhancement) was the same across all taste responses.
claims.source: That is, if a given neuron's activity was significantly altered by BLA→GCx, the direction of impact (suppression/enhancement) was the same across all taste responses.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: In vitro slice recordings have shown BLA projection neurons to synapse onto both pyramidal cells (PCs) and interneurons (INs).
claims.source: Given that in vitro slice recordings e.g. Haley et al., 2016; Haley et al., 2020 have shown BLA projection neurons to synapse onto both pyramidal cells (PCs) and interneurons (INs)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior in vitro research.

claims.claim: Putative INs showed significantly higher basal firing rates than did putative PCs.
claims.source: Consistent with a great deal of prior research (e.g. Quirk et al., 2009), putative INs showed (on average) significantly higher basal firing rates than did putative PCs (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Laser stimulation suppressed taste responses in approximately half of the neurons identified as PCs.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4C, laser stimulation suppressed taste responses in approximately half of the neurons identified as PCs (n = 21 [47%])
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Among putative INs, the impact of laser stimulation was almost always suppression (90%).
claims.source: but among putative INs, the impact was almost always suppression (n = 19/21 [90%]).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: BLA→GC projection neurons provide excitatory glutamatergic input to both PCs and INs.
claims.source: This result is consistent with data (e.g. Saper, 1982; Allen et al., 1991) suggesting that BLA→GC projection neurons provide excitatory glutamatergic input to both PCs and INs
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical research.

claims.claim: Some changes in PC responding came directly via loss of excitatory BLA input, and some as the indirect effect of a loss of input to inhibitory INs.
claims.source: it would be expected that some changes in PC responding came directly via loss of (excitatory) BLA input, and some as the indirect effect of a loss of input to inhibitory INs (Stone et al., 2011; Haley et al., 2016)
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: INs were impacted mostly by direct loss of BLA input because PCs in sensory cortices make fewer local connections.
claims.source: the fact that only a small portion of INs showed enhanced firing rates, meanwhile, likely reflects the fact that INs were impacted mostly by direct loss of BLA input (because PCs in sensory cortices make fewer local connections; see Zhang et al., 2014; Haley et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: BLA→GCx changed taste responsiveness, specificity, or palatability-related activity similarly for INs and PCs.
claims.source: Beyond this basic property, however, we observed no significant neuron-type differences—BLA→GCx changed taste responsiveness, specificity, or palatability-related activity similarly for INs and PCs (all Chi-Squared >0.05)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: There is little evidence of neuron-type specificity in GC taste coding.
claims.source: a result consistent with our previous studies showing little evidence of neuron-type specificity in GC taste coding (Katz et al., 2001; Fontanini and Katz, 2006; Jones et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research from the same laboratory.

claims.claim: The impact of BLA→GCx manipulation is qualitatively different from direct optogenetic perturbation of GC neurons.
claims.source: A comparison of our data with datasets previously collected in our lab (specifically, data collected as part of Mukherjee et al., 2019), however, allows us to reject this hypothesis, in that the impact of our manipulation is qualitatively different from direct optogenetic perturbation of GC neurons (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Direct activation of ArchT expressed in GC somas changes the taste responses of almost all of the neurons (91%).
claims.source: For one thing, our manipulation altered the taste responses of ~50% of recorded GC neurons (Figure 3A); direct activation of ArchT expressed in GC somas, meanwhile, changes the taste responses of almost all of the neurons (91% of the recorded population; Figure 5B1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 5B1.

claims.claim: 87.9% of the response changes caused by direct optical perturbation of GC neurons involve suppression of firing.
claims.source: The nature of the changes differs between the two preparations, as well: 87.9% of the response changes caused by direct optical perturbation of GC neurons involve suppression of firing (Figure 5B2)—a significantly different percentage than that caused by BLA→GCx in this experiment (60% in Figure 3C; X2 = 17.07, p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 5B2 and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: When GC somas are led to express ArchT channels, laser illumination of GC causes immediate, steeply developing changes that reach asymptote within ~250 ms.
claims.source: When GC somas are themselves led to express ArchT channels, in contrast, laser illumination of GC causes immediate, steeply developing changes that reach asymptote within ~250 ms.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The changes in GC activity observed in the current experiment were not caused by perturbation of GC somas.
claims.source: We conclude that the changes in GC activity observed in the current experiment were not caused by perturbation of GC somas.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison analyses shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: In the majority of cases, optogenetic perturbation of BLA-GC axonal activity impacted GC taste response only after substantial delays, leaving the initial 200 ms of the responses unaltered.
claims.source: As already noted, while the laser was turned on at the time of taste delivery, in the majority of cases optogenetic perturbation of BLA-GC axonal activity impacted GC taste response only after substantial delays, leaving the initial 200 ms of the responses unaltered (Figures 2 and 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 2 and 5C.

claims.claim: The distribution of laser impact latencies shows multiple peaks rather than being uniform or a simple decay function.
claims.source: Inspection of this panel reveals that the onset of changes caused by BLA→GCx is neither uniform nor a simple decay function (which would be the two most likely results if BLA input played no role in GC temporal coding). Instead, there are multiple peaks in the function, reflecting multiple 'most likely times' for the onset of perturbation-related changes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the distribution analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: One peak in the distribution of impact latencies appeared between 300 and 350 ms after taste delivery, and a second appeared approximately 750 ms after taste delivery.
claims.source: One such peak appeared between 300 and 350 ms after taste delivery, and a second appeared approximately 750 ms after taste delivery.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the distribution analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: A bi-modal fit of the impact latency data suggested the timing of peaks to be 347.28 ms (SD = 110) and 754.39 ms (SD = 179).
claims.source: A bi-modal fit of the data suggested the timing these peaks to be 347.28 (SD = 110) and 754.39 ms (SD = 179)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical modeling of the distribution data.

claims.claim: The bi-modal Gaussian fit produced a higher coefficient of determination than an exponential decay function for the impact latency data.
claims.source: and attempts to fit the data with an exponential decay function produced a lower coefficient of determination (an index of absolute goodness of a fit) than that of the Gaussian mixture model
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of model fits.

claims.claim: The error scores at each time bin were significantly smaller with the bi-modal Gaussian fit than those with exponential fit.
claims.source: moreover, the error scores at each time bin (i.e. estimated values – raw values) were significantly smaller with the bi-modal Gaussian fit than those with exponential fit (t(24) = −2.39, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of model fits.

claims.claim: Response enhancements predominate prior to the 2nd epoch, while response suppressions are equally likely afterward.
claims.source: Consistent with this observation, the nature of the perturbation's impact appears to shift around the time of the 2nd epoch (the time at which responses first become taste-specific, see Katz et al., 2001; Fontanini and Katz, 2006; Sadacca et al., 2012): response enhancements predominate prior to this point (Figure 6B1), while response suppressions are equally likely afterward (Figure 6B2)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Only 3 out of 41 firing-rate modulations (8%) were restricted to the identity epoch.
claims.source: Figure 6C disconfirms this possibility, showing that only 3 out of the 41 firing-rate modulations (i.e. 8%) were restricted to the identity epoch.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: There were 15 neurons that were impacted only when the palatability epoch began.
claims.source: There were, meanwhile, 15 neurons that were impacted only when the palatability epoch began.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The difference between epochs in terms of impact restriction is significant (X2 = 5.86, p<0.05).
claims.source: This difference between epochs is significant (X2 = 5.86, p<0.05)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: The majority of the effects of BLA→GCx are felt in the time period in which palatability-related processing is found.
claims.source: and it means that the majority of the effects of BLA→GCx are felt in the time period in which palatability-related processing is found.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: 2.5 s perturbations of BLA input to GC change taste-driven activity in ways that are both non-random and complex.
claims.source: In summary, 2.5 s perturbations of BLA input to GC change taste-driven activity in ways that are both non-random and complex—firing is modulated in specific relation to the dynamics that characterize GC taste processing.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analyses presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Taste responses in BLA contain only two epochs, with the early detection epoch transitioning directly into the palatability-rich information epoch at ~200 ms following taste delivery.
claims.source: Unlike taste responses in GC, those in BLA contain only two epochs, with the early detection epoch transitioning directly into the palatability-rich information epoch at ~200 ms following taste delivery (Fontanini et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The percentage of GC neurons responding in a taste-specific manner was identical (71.4%) in laser-off and laser-on trial types.
claims.source: While the perturbation did significantly change the firing rates of a large number (78 out of 140 in Figure 3) of neurons, we observed little evidence that BLA→GCx changed the incidence of taste-specific responses—the percentage of GC neurons responding in a taste-specific manner was identical (71.4%) in the two trial types (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The proportions of neurons responding to each taste are similar for Laser-Off and Laser-On trials.
claims.source: A closer look at this result revealed roughly similar distributions of individual taste responses in the two trial types (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: GC neurons are broadly tuned.
claims.source: Note that more than 50% of our GC sample responded to each taste; the fact that this percentage is far higher than 1/4 of 71.4% (the percentage of neurons that produced taste specific responses) means that GC neurons are broadly tuned—a result that is consistent with the vast majority of electrophysiological datasets involving >1–2 deliveries of each taste.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Figure 7B, supported by reference to prior research.

claims.claim: GC neurons remained broadly tuned even when BLA→GC axons were perturbed via optogenetic inhibition.
claims.source: GC neurons remained broadly tuned even when BLA→GC axons were perturbed via optogenetic inhibition, such that a chi-squared analysis failed to identify a significant difference between conditions (Laser Off vs. On; X2 = 2.78, p>0.05).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Similar numbers of taste responses were created and destroyed by BLA→GCx.
claims.source: Given the fact that BLA→GCx changed firing rates in GC taste responses (Figures 2–6), the results shown in Figure 7A and B imply that similar numbers of taste responses were created and destroyed by BLA→GCx. Figure 7C confirms this implication: several taste responses were lost when activity in BLA→GC axons was perturbed, but for each GC neuron for which taste specificity was lost, another neuron became a taste-specific neuron.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: BLA→GCx changed the specific composition of the neural ensembles producing taste-specific responses, but the tastes continued to be coded by similarly sized GC populations.
claims.source: Although BLA→GCx changed the specific composition of the neural ensembles producing taste-specific responses, the tastes continued to be coded by similarly sized GC populations when BLA input to GC was perturbed.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claims.claim: GC single-neuron activity was reliably taste-specific, with the classifier correctly identifying each administered taste on more than 50% of the held-out trials.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 7D, we failed to find substantial support for this hypothesis, in that BLA→GCx again proved to have little impact on the taste specificity of GC firing: the left panel confirms that GC single-neuron activity was reliably taste-specific—the classifier allowed us to correctly identify each administered taste (x-axis) on more than 50% of the held-out trials (y-axis), a percentage far higher than chance (25%).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the classification analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: An essentially identical classification result was obtained from trials in which BLA input to GC was perturbed.
claims.source: An essentially identical result was obtained from trials in which BLA input to GC was perturbed; furthermore, this held true regardless of whether we performed the analysis on whole-trial data or limited our analysis to firing within the Identity epoch.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the classification analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: When the classifier was trained and tested on trials within the same laser condition, 64% of control trials and 58% of perturbed trials were correctly classified.
claims.source: The results of this analysis are plain: when the classifier was trained and tested on trials within the same laser condition (the solid gray and green bars), 64% of control trials and 58% of perturbed trials were correctly classified—the patterns of performance, both well above chance, do not differ from one another, demonstrating that BLA→GCx had no deleterious impact on the quality of coding content (X2 = 2.96, p>0.05).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the classification analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Classification performance dropped when the classifier was tested and trained on different trial types.
claims.source: Classification performance dropped, however, when the classifier was tested and trained on different trial types (left hatched green bar; X2 = 5.22, p<0.05)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the classification analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Classification performance became significantly worse (45% correctness) when the analysis was focused on neurons for which firing rates were changed by the input perturbation.
claims.source: a reduction that became significantly worse (45% correctness; right hatched green bar) when the analysis was focused on neurons for which firing rates were changed by the input perturbation (X2 = 30.22, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the classification analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: While GC remains taste discriminative without BLA input, coding for taste identity is altered.
claims.source: Thus, while GC remains taste discriminative without BLA input, coding for taste identity is altered.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the classification analyses shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Inhibition of BLA→GC axons changes firing without having measurable impact on the magnitude of GC taste coding in the first ~750 ms of taste responses.
claims.source: But this result, whereby inhibition of BLA→GC axons changes firing without having measurable impact on the magnitude of GC taste coding in the first ~750 ms of taste responses, contrasts strongly with the result of this same perturbation on Late-epochal palatability-related activity.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement comparing the effects on identity and palatability coding.

claims.claim: The growth in firing-palatability correlation across the 2nd half-second after taste delivery in control trials is standard for GC taste responses.
claims.source: the growth in firing-palatability correlation across the 2nd half-second after taste delivery in control trials (black open circle) is standard for GC taste responses
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the example shown in Figure 8A2 and reference to prior knowledge.

claims.claim: In BLA→GCx trials, the palatability correlation rose more slowly, reached a lower asymptote, and disappeared more quickly than in control trials.
claims.source: but in BLA→GCx trials this correlation rose more slowly (red circles in Figure 8A2), reached a lower asymptote, and disappeared more quickly.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the example shown in Figure 8A2.

claims.claim: The number of neurons for which Late-epoch taste response firing rates were significantly correlated with palatability decreased with the perturbation.
claims.source: While in some cases BLA→GCx actually increased palatability-relatedness of GC neurons (see the example in Figure 8B1-2), overall the number of neurons for which Late-epoch taste response firing rates were significantly correlated with palatability decreased with the perturbation (Figure 8C; between-condition X2 = 5.49, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8C and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: A far larger number and percentage of neurons lost palatability-related firing with BLA→GCx than gained it.
claims.source: Figure 8D reveals further details, showing that a far larger number (and percentage) of neurons lost palatability-related firing with BLA→GCx than gained (compare Figure 8C & D to Figure 7A & C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: The correlation between firing and palatability was lower for Late epoch firing in perturbed trials.
claims.source: This result was corroborated by a direct comparison of the correlation between firing and palatability, which was lower—for Late epoch firing only—in perturbed trials (time x condition F(1,139) = 5.70, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: There was an overall loss of palatability-related firing in GC, in the absence of significant loss of identity-related information, when input from BLA was perturbed.
claims.source: Clearly, there was an overall loss of palatability-related firing in GC, in the absence of significant loss of identity-related information, when input from BLA was perturbed.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analyses shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claims.claim: The emergence of Late-epoch palatability coding is revealed to be a sudden transition into a new ensemble state, in which firing-rate changes occur simultaneously in multiple GC neurons.
claims.source: as previously discussed, the emergence of Late-epoch palatability coding is revealed, using single-trial analyses involving Hidden Markov Modeling (HMM), to be a sudden transition into a new ensemble state, in which firing-rate changes occur simultaneously in multiple GC neurons (Jones et al., 2007; Miller and Katz, 2010; Sadacca et al., 2016)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research using HMM analyses.

claims.claim: The sudden transition into palatability-related firing directly drives behavior.
claims.source: it is this sudden transition itself that directly drives behavior (Mukherjee et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The ensemble firing-rate transitions occurred suddenly in control trials, reflecting the simultaneous precipitous changes in firing rates in multiple neurons, but varied in latency from trial to trial.
claims.source: As we have observed previously, the ensemble firing-rate transitions (the most likely times of state changes) occurred suddenly in control trials, reflecting the simultaneous precipitous changes in firing rates in multiple neurons, but varied in latency from trial to trial (e.g. Jones et al., 2007; Moran and Katz, 2014; Sadacca et al., 2016; Mukherjee et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the HMM analysis shown in Figure 9A and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The transition into palatability-correlated firing was far less steep in BLA→GCx trials than in control trials.
claims.source: When we brought the same analysis routine to bear in trials in which activity in BLA→GC axons was perturbed (Figure 9B1, dashed red line), the transition into palatability-correlated firing was far less steep than that in control trials from the very same sessions (and same neural ensembles).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the HMM analysis shown in Figure 9B1.

claims.claim: The slope of the rise into palatability-correlatedness was significantly lower for trials in which the laser was turned on than for trials in which the laser was off.
claims.source: To quantify this finding for statistical evaluation, we fitted sigmoid curves to each transition function (black and red solid lines), and found that the slope of the rise into palatability-correlatedness was significantly lower for trials in which the laser was turned on than for trials in which the laser was off (as indicated by the lack of overlap between the 95% credible intervals in Figure 9B2; see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 9B2.

claims.claim: With activity in BLA→GC axons perturbed, GC ensemble taste activity fails to transition with normal suddenness into palatability-related firing.
claims.source: This result makes it clear that, with activity in BLA→GC axons perturbed, GC ensemble taste activity fails to transition with normal suddenness into palatability-related firing.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the HMM analyses shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: The slope of the fitting line for single-neuron firing rate changes was significantly shallower than 1 (unity).
claims.source: These data would be expected to hover close to the gray dashed 'unity' (slope = 1) line in this plot if BLA→GCx failed to influence the precipitousness of single-neuron firing rate changes; in fact, however, a regression analysis of the data revealed that slope (0.42) of the fitting line to be significantly shallower than 1 (p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claims.claim: Perturbation of activity in BLA→GC axons reduced the rate of firing rate changes across most slope intervals.
claims.source: To probe further, we grouped the data into intervals of slope ranges calculated in control trials (Figure 10C); perturbation of activity in BLA→GC axons reduced the rate of firing rate changes (ps < 0.05) across most of these intervals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 10C.

claims.claim: The firing rate changes of most neurons in an ensemble were 'blurred' in the vicinity of the transition into palatability-related firing when BLA→GC axon activity was perturbed.
claims.source: This pattern of results strongly supports the hypothesis that the firing rate changes of most neurons in an ensemble were 'blurred' in the vicinity of the transition into palatability-related firing when BLA→GC axon activity was perturbed.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analyses shown in Figure 10B-C.

claims.claim: Disconnecting GC from BLA kept the single neurons within the GC network from changing their firing rates quickly in the vicinity of the transition into palatability-relatedness.
claims.source: In other words, disconnecting GC from BLA kept the single neurons within the GC network from changing their firing rates quickly in the vicinity of the transition into palatability-relatedness; this in turn explains the loss of suddenness in the GC ensemble transition into the Palatability state.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion from the analyses shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: The spread of the distribution of maximal slope times did not differ significantly between laser-off and laser-on conditions.
claims.source: Figure 10D shows the result of this analysis. While inspection of the figure reveals a good deal of noise in the distributions (likely the result of the small sample), it does not suggest any major differences in the spread of the distribution. Certainly the difference between distributions failed to reach significance (X2 = 13.93, p>0.05)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 10D.

claims.claim: The coherence of the timing of the GC response dynamic has not been altered by the perturbation of BLA→GC projections.
claims.source: indicating that the coherence of the timing of the GC response dynamic has not been altered by the perturbation of BLA→GC projections, a result consistent with the analysis that found comparable means of the distributions between each trial type (OFF vs ON trials: −17.98 ± 5.29 ms vs. −16.23 ± 5.51 ms).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 10D.

claims.claim: The loss of the normally observed sharp ensemble transitions into palatability-related firing appears to not reflect decoupling of still sharp single-neuron transitions, but rather an alteration of the basic functioning of the networks.
claims.source: Overall, the loss of the normally observed sharp ensemble transitions into palatability-related firing appears to not reflect decoupling of still sharp single-neuron transitions, but rather an alteration of the basic functioning of the networks, such that entire ensembles of neurons fail to cleanly transition from one state to the next.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analyses shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: The impact of BLA→GCx on slopes changes during state transition times is not universal but epoch-dependent.
claims.source: The impact of BLA→GCx on slopes changes during state transition times is not universal but epoch-dependent.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement introducing the analysis of identity epoch transitions.

claims.claim: BLA→GCx has very little impact on either the sharpness or timing of firing-rate changes during transitions into the identity state.
claims.source: We repeated the same analysis depicted in Figure 10A on firing rate changes comprising transitions into the identity state (which typically occurred 100–600 ms after taste delivery). We found very little impact of BLA→GCx on either the sharpness or timing of these firing-rate changes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 11.

claims.claim: The fit line for identity state transition slopes did not differ significantly from unity.
claims.source: Figure 11A displays the slopes of this earlier transition for each neuron, with control trials plotted against perturbed trials. As revealed by a regression analysis, the fit line (slope = 0.79; red solid line) did not differ significantly from unity (p>0.05), indicating that the perturbation has little impact on the firing rate changes when the ensemble is transitioning into the identity state.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis shown in Figure 11A.

claims.claim: An ANOVA conducted on identity state transition slopes revealed no significant main effect of Laser and no significant interaction.
claims.source: This null effect was confirmed when the range of slopes observed in control trials was divided into subgroups (Figure 11B); an ANOVA conducted on these data revealed no significant main effect of Laser (F(1,58) = 1.44, p>0.05) and no significant interaction (F < 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 11B.

claims.claim: BLA→GCx does not alter the dynamics of firing changes during identity state transitions.
claims.source: When examining the timing of sharpest slope changes relative to transition times (Figure 11C), we also found no evidence indicating that BLA→GCx alters the dynamics of firing changes (X2 = 20.06, p>0.05).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 11C.

claims.claim: The input from BLA critically modulates the dynamics of GC taste response by altering palatability-related activity while leaving the identity processing relatively intact.
claims.source: Overall, this pattern of results further confirms that the input from BLA critically modulates the dynamics of GC taste response by altering palatability-related activity while leaving the identity processing relatively intact.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analyses shown in Figures 10 and 11.

claims.claim: GC taste processing is complex, involving a sequence of firing rate transformations that chart the evolution of responses from reporting the presence of stimuli on the tongue, to discriminating the taste identity, and then finally to generating affective responses.
claims.source: In summary, as revealed in our 20 years of research, taste processing in GC is complex, involving a sequence of firing rate transformations that chart the evolution of those responses from reporting the presence of stimuli on the tongue, to discriminating the taste identity, and then finally to generating affective responses.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement drawing on the authors' research program.

claims.claim: The nature of the dynamic GC taste processing process almost necessarily requires that GC collaborates with other brain regions.
claims.source: The nature of this dynamic process almost necessarily requires that GC collaborates with other brain regions
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the complexity of GC taste processing.

claims.claim: GC palatability-related activity is organized by connections to GC from BLA.
claims.source: and while such a collaboration could simply involve information passage from one area to another, the results of the current research suggest that GC palatability-related activity is organized by connections to GC from BLA.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Taste system functions as a nonlinear 'attractor network' in which taste responses evolve through a sequence of discrete, quasi-stationary 'states'.
claims.source: These studies (e.g. Jones et al., 2007; Miller and Katz, 2010; Escola et al., 2011; Mazzucato et al., 2015; Mazzucato et al., 2019; La Camera et al., 2019) suggest that the taste system functions as a nonlinear 'attractor network,' in which (as we have again shown) taste responses evolve through a sequence of discrete, quasi-stationary 'states,'
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical neuroscience studies.

claims.claim: The transitions between taste response states are jointly determined by the strength of both the attractors and noise impinging upon the network.
claims.source: and that the transitions between these states are jointly determined by the strength of both the attractors and noise impinging upon the network (Miller and Katz, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical research.

claims.claim: BLA is an essential part of the dynamical system underlying taste processing.
claims.source: We hypothesize that BLA is an essential part of this dynamical system
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental results.

claims.claim: The loss of BLA input may reduce the nonlinearity of the attractor dynamics and predispose the network to random noise.
claims.source: and that, given the critical involvement of BLA in palatability processing, the loss of BLA input may reduce the nonlinearity of the attractor dynamics (and to predispose the network to random noise).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claims.claim: During taste processing, BLA actively interacts with GC and coordinates activity among cortical neurons, so that the cortical ensemble can transition suddenly and coherently into the palatability state.
claims.source: Based on our results, it is reasonable to speculate that during taste processing, BLA actively interacts with GC and coordinates activity among cortical neurons, so that the cortical ensemble can transition suddenly and coherently into the palatability state.

claims.source: Finally, given the nonlinearity of this dynamic population effect, and the dense reciprocal connections between BLA and GC, their interaction is unlikely to be unidirectional, a suggestion that receives support from an earlier study demonstrating that electrical stimulating GC can alter BLA taste responses (Yamamoto et al., 1984; also see Lavi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior research.

results.result: AAV-mediated ArchT expression in BLA resulted in anterograde labeling of axons in GC without cell body expression in GC, confirming pathway-specific targeting. The dataset comprised 140 neurons from 4 rats with confirmed viral expression and electrode placement.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 provide converging anatomical and methodological validation. Immunohistochemical data (C24) confirms selective axonal expression in GC, anterograde transport is demonstrated (C25), and sample size is clearly stated (C26). These establish the technical foundation for subsequent experiments.

results.result: The impact of BLA→GC axon perturbation on GC neurons was consistent across two recording sessions, with no significant differences in percentage of affected neurons, direction of impact, or strength of impact between sessions, suggesting taste novelty plays minimal role.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 report statistical analyses showing session consistency (all X² <1, F=1.95 p>0.05). The inference about taste novelty (C29) is reasonable given the lack of session differences. This justifies pooling data across sessions for subsequent analyses.

results.result: Optogenetic perturbation of BLA→GC axons strongly altered GC taste responses in complex, neuron-specific ways. The impact was not a simple reduction in firing but showed reliable directional effects (enhancement or suppression) within individual neurons, with delayed onset that spared the initial 150-200ms and aligned with known GC taste response epoch timing.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C36 describe the basic phenomenology of the perturbation effect with supporting data from Figure 2. The heatmap analysis (C32) demonstrates within-neuron consistency, and temporal analyses (C34-C36) show epoch-aligned effects. These observations are well-documented and form the basis for subsequent detailed analyses.

results.result: BLA→GC axon perturbation impacted 55.7% of recorded GC neurons, with 46.1% showing changes to all four taste stimuli. Approximately 40% of individual taste responses were affected, and critically, when multiple taste responses in a neuron were impacted, the direction of change (suppression or enhancement) was consistent across all affected responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C41 provide quantitative characterization supported by data in Figure 3. The consistency of directional effects within neurons (C40-C41) is particularly important for understanding the nature of BLA→GC influence. Statistical support is provided throughout.

results.result: Cell-type analysis revealed differential effects of BLA→GC perturbation: putative interneurons showed predominantly suppression (90%), while putative pyramidal cells showed mixed effects (47% suppression). This pattern is consistent with BLA providing excitatory glutamatergic input to both cell types, though functional coding properties were similarly affected across cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C50 integrate prior in vitro findings (C42, C46) with current in vivo observations (C43-C45, C49). The differential directional effects (C44-C45) are well-explained by circuit architecture (C47-C48), though these mechanistic interpretations are inferences. The lack of cell-type specificity in coding (C49-C50) is statistically supported.

results.result: The effects of BLA→GC axon perturbation were qualitatively distinct from direct GC soma perturbation. Direct GC perturbation affected 91% of neurons (vs. 50% for axon perturbation), showed 88% suppression (vs. 60%), and produced immediate effects reaching asymptote within 250ms (vs. delayed effects for axon perturbation).
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 provide critical control analyses using comparison data from prior work (Mukherjee et al., 2019). The quantitative differences in percentage affected (C52), direction (C53), and temporal dynamics (C54) are statistically significant and rule out off-target GC soma effects. The conclusion (C55) is well-justified.

results.result: Despite tonic 2.5s laser stimulation, the impact of BLA→GC perturbation was epoch-specific. The distribution of impact latencies showed multiple peaks at ~347ms and ~754ms (better fit by bi-modal Gaussian than exponential decay), aligning with identity and palatability epoch onsets. Effects were predominantly felt during the palatability epoch, with only 8% of modulations restricted to the identity epoch versus significantly more (19%) restricted to the palatability epoch.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C67 demonstrate a key finding: tonic perturbation produces temporally structured effects. Statistical model comparison (C59-C61) supports bi-modal distribution over exponential decay. The epoch-specific analysis (C62-C66) with statistical support (C65: X²=5.86, p<0.05) shows preferential palatability epoch impact. This is a major mechanistic insight.

results.result: BLA→GC perturbation did not reduce the incidence of taste-specific responses in GC—71.4% of neurons remained taste-specific in both conditions. While the specific composition of taste-responsive ensembles changed (with similar numbers of responses created and destroyed), population-level taste coding was preserved.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 demonstrate preserved identity coding at the population level despite single-neuron changes. The identical percentages (C69), similar distributions (C70, C72), and balanced gain/loss (C73) are well-documented in Figure 7A-C. This dissociation between firing rate changes and coding capacity is important.

results.result: Classification analyses confirmed that taste identity remained discriminable during BLA→GC perturbation (>50% correct, well above 25% chance). Within-condition classification was similar for control (64%) and perturbed (58%) trials. However, cross-condition classification dropped significantly, especially for neurons with altered firing rates (45% correct), indicating that while GC remains discriminative, the coding scheme is altered.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 provide sophisticated computational analysis of coding. Within-condition performance (C77) shows preserved discriminability, but cross-condition deficits (C78-C79) reveal altered coding schemes. Statistical support is provided (X² values, p-values). The conclusion (C80) appropriately distinguishes between coding capacity and coding implementation.

results.result: BLA→GC perturbation significantly reduced palatability-related activity in the late epoch. The number of palatability-correlated neurons decreased from 33.6% to 25.0% (X²=5.49, p<0.05), with far more neurons losing than gaining palatability responses. Palatability correlations rose more slowly, reached lower asymptotes, and disappeared more quickly in perturbed trials, specifically during the late epoch.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C87 demonstrate selective impairment of palatability coding with statistical support (C84, C86). The temporal specificity (late epoch only) and asymmetric gain/loss (C85) are well-documented in Figure 8. This contrasts sharply with preserved identity coding and represents a major functional dissociation.

results.result: Hidden Markov Modeling revealed that BLA→GC perturbation disrupted the normal sudden, coherent transition into palatability-related firing. While control trials showed sharp ensemble transitions (with trial-to-trial variability in timing), perturbed trials showed significantly shallower transitions into palatability-correlated states, as quantified by non-overlapping 95% credible intervals for sigmoid slope parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C93 employ sophisticated ensemble analysis (HMM) to reveal network-level effects. The prior work establishing sudden transitions (C88-C90) provides context. The current finding of reduced transition sharpness (C91-C92) is statistically rigorous using Bayesian credible intervals. This is a key mechanistic finding about BLA's role in organizing ensemble dynamics.

results.result: Single-neuron analysis revealed that BLA→GC perturbation reduced the sharpness of individual neurons' firing rate changes during palatability state transitions. Regression analysis showed slopes significantly shallower than unity (0.42, p<0.05), with reductions across most slope intervals. This 'blurring' of single-neuron transitions explains the loss of ensemble transition sharpness.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 test the mechanism underlying ensemble effects. The regression analysis (C94) and binned analysis (C95) provide converging evidence with statistical support. The interpretation (C96-C97) that reduced single-neuron sharpness explains ensemble effects is well-justified by the data in Figure 10B-C.

results.result: The timing coherence of GC ensemble responses was not altered by BLA→GC perturbation. The distribution of maximal slope times did not differ significantly between conditions (X²=13.93, p>0.05), with comparable means and standard deviations. This indicates that the loss of sharp transitions reflects altered single-neuron dynamics rather than temporal decoupling of neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 test an alternative hypothesis about ensemble disruption. The statistical analysis (C98) with supporting distributional comparisons (C99) rules out temporal decoupling. The conclusion (C100) appropriately distinguishes between two mechanisms and is supported by the data in Figure 10D.

results.result: The impact of BLA→GC perturbation on firing rate transition sharpness was epoch-specific. During identity state transitions (100-600ms), perturbation had minimal effect: regression slopes did not differ from unity (0.79, p>0.05), ANOVA showed no laser effect (F(1,58)=1.44, p>0.05), and timing was unaltered (X²=20.06, p>0.05). This contrasts with strong effects on palatability transitions.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C106 demonstrate functional specificity by showing null effects on identity epoch transitions. Multiple statistical tests (regression, ANOVA, chi-square) converge on the same conclusion. This epoch-specific pattern (Figure 11) strengthens the interpretation that BLA specifically organizes palatability-related dynamics.

results.result: Optogenetic perturbation of BLA→GC axons during taste delivery strongly altered GC taste responses in an epoch-specific manner, reducing palatability-related activity in the late epoch without reducing taste identity information in the middle epoch, and diminishing the abruptness of ensemble transitions into the late epoch. These results suggest BLA 'organizes' behavior-related GC taste dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7 summarize the main experimental findings. Each component is supported by detailed analyses in subsequent results: epoch-specific effects (C4), selective palatability impairment (C5), and disrupted ensemble transitions (C6). The organizational role conclusion (C7) is an appropriate inference from the pattern of results, though 'organizes' is somewhat interpretive.

results.result: The authors conclude that GC palatability-related activity is organized by connections from BLA, with BLA actively coordinating activity among cortical neurons to enable sudden, coherent transitions into the palatability state. This represents a specific organizational role rather than simple information relay.
results.evaluation: Claims C109, C114, C118 represent the main interpretive conclusions. These are well-supported by the experimental findings: selective palatability impairment, preserved identity coding, reduced transition sharpness at single-neuron and ensemble levels, and epoch-specific effects. The 'organizational' interpretation is justified, though alternative mechanisms cannot be fully ruled out.

results.result: The authors propose that the taste system functions as a nonlinear attractor network where BLA is an essential component, and that loss of BLA input may reduce the nonlinearity of attractor dynamics and predispose the network to random noise, explaining the observed blurring of transitions.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C113 invoke attractor network theory to explain results. While C110-C111 cite theoretical work, C112-C113 are explicitly speculative hypotheses. The attractor framework is plausible and consistent with the data, but the specific mechanisms (reduced nonlinearity, increased noise susceptibility) are not directly tested. This remains a theoretical interpretation requiring future validation.

results.result: Based on prior work showing that GC inhibition during the first 500ms delays palatability-driven behavior, combined with earlier palatability coding in BLA than GC, the authors speculate that BLA-GC interactions across 0.5-1.0s are responsible for causing the transition into the GC palatability epoch.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 integrate prior findings (C115 from Mukherjee et al., 2019) with current results to propose a temporal mechanism. While the inference (C116) from prior work is reasonable, the specific timing hypothesis (C117) is explicitly speculative. The current data show BLA is important for palatability transitions but don't directly test the proposed 0.5-1.0s interaction window.

results.result: The introduction and discussion establish the scientific context: palatability drives consumption decisions, GC shows dynamic taste processing through sequential epochs with sudden transitions that predict behavior, GC likely requires network interactions given response complexity, and BLA is anatomically and functionally positioned to interact with GC in palatability processing, though prior pharmacological studies had limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C23, C68, C107-C108, C119 provide background knowledge and rationale. These are well-supported by extensive citations to prior literature. The critiques of prior pharmacological approaches (C22-C23) appropriately motivate the current optogenetic approach. This contextual material is accurate and appropriately cited.
